attacks.claim: The cost math treats a per-day token volume as monthly. 38M lines x 60 tokens is 2.28B tokens per day, which at $0.50/1M is about $1,140 per day, or roughly $34k per month before output and before peak days. That is more than 20x the approved $1,500/month budget.
attacks.evidence: Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140 ... Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget.

attacks.claim: Cost excludes the fixed prompt, which is re-sent in each of 8,640 calls per day, and it summarises idle services every 5 minutes with no skip logic. Both add unbudgeted input spend.
attacks.evidence: every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt

attacks.claim: The headline MTTR target (47 to 30 min) has no baseline breakdown showing how much time is spent grepping, and no prototype. The replay eval grades summary usefulness, not MTTR impact, and relies on hindsight grading by the incident commander.
attacks.evidence: Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min within one quarter of launch.

attacks.claim: The 40-incident replay assumes the logs and redaction rules from those past incidents still exist and match current behaviour. The plan does not verify this.
attacks.evidence: replay the last 40 incidents: for each, generate the summary that would have been attached at page time

attacks.claim: Redaction is described as covering only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs. Names, customer identifiers and free-text payload PII are not addressed, yet the logs are sent to an external LLM. Zero retention is asserted rather than verified.
attacks.evidence: already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)

attacks.claim: The design depends on a single external model vendor with no fallback model, no self-hosted option, no stated processing region, and no exit plan.
attacks.evidence: Model: Corvid-mini, $0.50 per 1M input tokens, $2.00 per 1M output tokens.

attacks.claim: Peak volume is 1.6x average and the summariser has no stated handling for rate limits, batching, or per-window context-window overflow from noisy services. At peak, each 5-minute window carries roughly 12M input tokens across services.
attacks.evidence: Application logs: 38M lines/day average across 30 services (peak day 61M).

attacks.claim: log-tap is a new subscriber on the shared Vector pipeline. A slow summariser or queue could back-pressure log forwarding for all services. There is no LLM outage or timeout behaviour and no alerting on summariser health.
attacks.evidence: subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage and forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue.

attacks.claim: Summaries are pre-computed on a 5-minute cadence, so the one attached at page time can be up to 5 minutes plus LLM latency stale and may miss the onset of the incident. This contradicts the stated goal of a summary within seconds of a page.
attacks.evidence: Give the on-call engineer a plain-language 'what is going wrong right now' summary within seconds of a page

attacks.claim: No feature flag or kill switch is described for log-tap or for PagerDuty comment posting. 'Advisory only' is a policy statement, not a technical control.
attacks.evidence: Summaries are advisory only. Alert rules, paging, and escalation policies are unchanged.

attacks.claim: Log lines contain attacker-influenced strings, and the LLM output is posted into PagerDuty and stored. Prompt injection through log content could plant misleading root-cause or 'suspected deploy' text in on-call tooling. There is no output sanitisation or API key handling spec.
attacks.evidence: sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM ... stores a structured summary ... auto-comment with the latest summaries

attacks.claim: Application logs, which may contain customer data, are sent to a third-party processor. The plan cites an internal DPA but does not confirm that customer contracts or subprocessor disclosures permit this, nor the retention rules for stored summaries.
attacks.evidence: Corvid account has zero-retention enabled; data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417).

attacks.claim: The 'suspected deploy' field has no specified data source. Causal claims generated by the LLM are not grounded in deploy data, and the eval does not test for hallucinated deploys or endpoints.
attacks.evidence: structured summary (top errors, new error signatures, affected endpoints, suspected deploy)

attacks.claim: There is no on-call user input on what the summary must contain or whether it beats existing dashboards. The plan assumes the grep time is the core problem.
attacks.evidence: instead of spending the first 15-20 minutes grepping logs across 30 services

attacks.claim: Summaries are auto-posted into PagerDuty incidents, which may add noise to the incident timeline during high-stress responses. The plan does not discuss length or frequency limits on those comments.
attacks.evidence: the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries for the paging service and its direct dependencies

attacks.claim: Dashboards are listed as a work item, but the plan has no specification for them.
Output is rendered as PagerDuty comments with no spec for formatting, length, or scannability under incident stress. This is a minor concern rather than a demonstrated barrier.
attacks.evidence: the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries

attacks.claim: The fixed prompt has no versioning or eval gate for changes. The 'direct dependencies' data comes from a service catalog whose freshness is not addressed.
attacks.evidence: with a fixed prompt ... (from the service catalog)

attacks.claim: Staffing assumes both engineers are full-time for 6 weeks, but the charter puts on-call/interrupt work at about 50% of their time. Effective capacity is roughly 6 eng-weeks against 12 planned, with no contingency in the estimate.
attacks.evidence: Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks).
